title: Worsening breathlessness in a 78-year-old retired biologist
desc: This station is a focused breathlessness history and cardiorespiratory examination of Kathy Jefferson, a 78-year-old retired biologist seeing her GP. She has 2 months of breathlessness that has got much worse over the past week, with orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and she had an NSTEMI 6 months ago. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, ECG, chest X-ray report and blood results. They should diagnose new decompensated congestive heart failure (NYHA class IV) with pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions, arrange transfer to hospital, explain heart failure to her and safety-net.
focus: Dyspnoea: quantifying breathlessness by exercise tolerance and screening other systems with cluster questions, then recognising decompensated congestive heart failure on the chest X-ray, ECG and bloods, and arranging hospital care
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Kathy Jefferson is a 78-year-old retired biologist who has come in because her breathlessness is getting worse. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first and is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Jefferson and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her ECG, her chest X-ray report and her blood results. Interpret them in a handover, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, outline your management approach, explain the problem to Mrs Jefferson and give safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Kathy Jefferson, a 78-year-old retired biologist. Date of birth: 14 March 1948 (78). You are sitting upright in the chair and are a little short of breath. You talk in full sentences but pause for breath now and then. You are calm, articulate and interested in what is going on. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My breathing's been getting worse, doctor. I just can't seem to get a full breath in."

The breathlessness (give only when asked):

  • Onset and course: it started about 2 months ago and has got much worse over the past week.
  • Quality: "I just can't get a full breath in."
  • How far you can walk: 2 months ago you got breathless walking about 50 m ("when walking down the block"). In the past week you get breathless after about 5 m ("walking from the bedroom to the kitchen").
  • Better: "Not that I have noticed."
  • Worse: lying down.
  • Only if asked specifically:
    • Orthopnoea: yes. You now sleep propped up on 3 pillows because you get breathless lying flat.
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea: yes. Several times this week you have woken at night gasping for breath and had to sit on the edge of the bed until it passed.
    Do not volunteer either of these.
  • Impact: you are finding basic chores around the house difficult.
  • What you think it is: "I'm not sure."

Other symptoms (only if asked; all are absent):

  • Heart: no ankle swelling that you have noticed, no cough, no discomfort under the right ribs. No chest pain or tightness, no sweating, no feeling of doom, no nausea or vomiting. No palpitations. No fainting or near-fainting, including on exertion.
  • Infection: no fever, chills or shivers. No cough or phlegm. No sharp pain on breathing in.
  • Airways: no wheeze, no long-standing cough, no night-time cough. No hay fever or eczema, and no asthma as a child.
  • Lung scarring: no dry cough. You worked in a university laboratory with no dust, asbestos or heavy chemical exposure. You have never had radiotherapy.
  • Clot: no coughing up blood, no calf pain or swelling, no recent long trips or operations.
  • Thyroid: no anxiety, tremor, weight loss or diarrhoea.
  • Anaemia: not tired as such, "just can't get my breath". No one has said you look pale. No palpitations.
  • Weight: you have not weighed yourself recently.

Past medical history:

  • High blood pressure, diagnosed 14 years ago, now well controlled.
  • High cholesterol, diagnosed 12 years ago, now well controlled.
  • In hospital 6 months ago with a heart attack, which the doctors called an "NSTEMI". If asked about the details or any procedures, you don't remember them well. The discharge letter is with the GP.

Medications: aspirin, amlodipine and atorvastatin. You don't know the doses. No over-the-counter medicines or supplements, and no recreational drugs.

Allergies: none. Vaccinations: up to date.

Family history:

  • Your mother died of a heart attack at 72.
  • Your father had asthma from childhood.
  • Your sister has angina, which started when she was 58.
  • Your brother was diagnosed with high blood pressure at 38.
  • Your children are healthy.

Social history:

  • Smoking: you started at 25, about 10 cigarettes a day (half a pack), and stopped after 20 years (at 45).
  • Alcohol: social and occasional.
  • Exercise: minimal, and now limited even more by the breathlessness.
  • Diet: takeaway twice a week, otherwise healthy.
  • Home and support: you live with your daughter's family in a middle-class suburb and are well connected with friends and family.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are not sure what is causing this. You are worried because you can't manage simple chores and don't want to be a burden on your daughter. You would like to know what is going on and to get your breath back.

Question to raise (near the end of Part 1, if not already covered): "Could this have anything to do with my heart attack?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: older woman sitting upright, mildly breathless at rest and pausing for breath mid-sentence. Not cyanosed, not pale, not distressed. Alert and oriented.
  • Vital signs (09:30): HR 104 beats/min, regular; BP 156/88 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 94% on room air; temperature 36.7 °C. Weight 70 kg today; the practice record shows 67 kg 3 months ago.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds. No clubbing, no nicotine staining, no tremor. Radial pulse regular, normal character.
  • Face and eyes: no conjunctival pallor, no central cyanosis, no lid lag or exophthalmos.
  • Neck: JVP raised 5 cm above the sternal angle, with a positive hepatojugular reflux. Carotid pulse normal in volume and upstroke (not slow-rising). Trachea midline. No goitre.
  • Praecordium: apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. No heave or thrill. Heart sounds S1 and S2 with a third heart sound (S3 gallop). No murmurs; specifically, no ejection systolic murmur and nothing radiating to the carotids.
  • Chest: expansion reduced at both bases. Dull to percussion at both bases, stony dull at the lowest part. Reduced breath sounds at both bases, with fine end-inspiratory crackles in both lower zones extending to the mid zones. No wheeze, no bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft. Liver edge not palpable, no right upper quadrant tenderness.
  • Legs and sacrum: no pitting oedema of the ankles, shins or sacrum. Calves soft, non-tender and equal in size.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms the patient's name and date of birth, explains confidentiality and gains consent for the history and examination.
Starts with an open question and builds rapport. Acknowledges how the breathlessness is affecting her chores, uses plain language and summarises back to her.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:

kids.x: Onset and course: started 2 months ago, much worse over the past week.
Quality: "can't get a full breath in".
Quantifies it by exercise tolerance, not a score out of 10: 50 m (down the block) 2 months ago, now about 5 m (bedroom to kitchen).
kids.d: Asking only for a rating out of 10 does not earn this item.

kids.x: Aggravating and relieving factors: worse lying down; nothing relieves it.

check.x: Asks specifically about orthopnoea (3 pillows) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (wakes gasping) and finds both.
check.d: Orthopnoea and PND are not volunteered. Credit only if the candidate asks about them specifically.

check.x: Asks about other heart failure features: ankle swelling, cough and right upper quadrant discomfort (all absent).
Asks about the impact on daily life (difficulty with basic chores) and what she thinks is causing it (not sure).
Uses cluster questions to screen differentials across systems:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least 5 diagnoses from different systems; part credit for 3 or 4. Items 6 and 7 together count as the heart failure cluster. Sub-item 1 must be covered.

kids.x: Ischaemia (ACS or angina): chest pain, sweating, nausea, sense of doom (none).
Aortic stenosis or arrhythmia: exertional chest pain or syncope, palpitations, fainting (none).
Pneumonia or TB: fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic pain (none).
COPD, asthma or interstitial lung disease: chronic or night-time cough, wheeze, atopy, occupational, chemical or radiotherapy exposure (none).
Pulmonary embolism: haemoptysis, pleuritic pain, calf swelling, immobility (none).
Thyrotoxicosis or anaemia: tremor, anxiety, weight loss, diarrhoea; fatigue, pallor (none).

check.x: Past medical history: hypertension (14 years) and hypercholesterolaemia (12 years), both well controlled, and admission with an NSTEMI 6 months ago.
check.d: The NSTEMI is the critical element.

check.x: Medications (aspirin, amlodipine, atorvastatin; no over-the-counter medicines, supplements or recreational drugs), allergies (none) and vaccinations (up to date).
Family history: mother died of AMI at 72, sister with angina from 58, brother with hypertension from 38, father with childhood asthma, children healthy.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified: about 10 a day from 25 for 20 years (about 10 pack-years), stopped at 45. Alcohol social and occasional.
Exercise (minimal), diet (takeaway twice a week), lives with her daughter's family, well supported.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including her worry about chores and whether this is linked to her heart attack.
Examination

General inspection, vital signs including SpO2 and weight. Finds her breathless at rest, sitting upright, with HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air and BP 156/88. Notes her weight is up 3 kg in 3 months.
check.d: Critical elements: recognises abnormal RR, HR and SpO2 at rest. Weight gain is supporting.

check.x: Examines the hands, pulse, eyes and neck for perfusion, pulse rhythm and character, clubbing, pallor, cyanosis, tremor and goitre (all normal).
Assesses the JVP (raised 5 cm) and hepatojugular reflux (positive).
Examines the praecordium. Finds a displaced apex beat and an S3, and listens specifically for the murmur of aortic stenosis, including at the carotids (none), with a normal carotid upstroke.
check.d: Critical element: auscultates and reports the S3 and the absence of a murmur. Explicit mention of the carotids is supporting.

check.x: Examines the chest front and back. Finds bibasal fine crackles extending to the mid zones, with dullness and reduced breath sounds at both bases, and no wheeze.
Looks for oedema at the ankles, shins and sacrum (none), hepatomegaly (none) and calf swelling or tenderness (none).
Interpretation
Observations: persisting tachycardia, tachypnoea and SpO2 93 to 94% on room air, worse after a short walk; hypertensive; afebrile. States she is not stable enough for outpatient care.
Chest X-ray, read systematically:
check.d: Source marking: cardiomegaly; bilateral pleural effusions; upper lobe diversion and batwing alveolar oedema; diffuse opacity in the lung fields. Accept in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. The candidate may confirm the film is today's PA; this is not scored.

kids.x: Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5).
Pulmonary oedema: upper lobe venous diversion, perihilar (batwing) alveolar oedema and diffuse opacity in the lung fields, with Kerley B lines.
kids.d: Upper lobe diversion and alveolar oedema are needed; Kerley B lines are supporting.

kids.x: Bilateral pleural effusions (blunted costophrenic angles).

check.x: ECG: sinus tachycardia with LVH and lateral strain pattern, unchanged from 6 months ago; no acute ST change and no AF.
Bloods: BNP 1,280 strongly supports heart failure; creatinine up from baseline 88 to 104 (eGFR 44); normal Hb and TSH make anaemia and thyrotoxicosis unlikely.

States the most likely diagnosis: new, decompensated congestive heart failure with pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions, probably ischaemic (NSTEMI 6 months ago) and hypertensive. Justifies it with the orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, S3, crackles, X-ray and BNP.
Classifies her as NYHA class IV (breathless at rest and on minimal activity, about 5 m from bedroom to kitchen).
check.d: The source answer is NYHA class IV.

check.x: Gives at least two differentials, each with one feature for or against (accept aortic stenosis/valve disease, recurrent ischaemia/ACS, COPD, PE).
check.d: The source's top three are heart failure, aortic stenosis or other valvulopathies, and COPD.

check.x: Management
Decides with the supervising GP that she needs hospital care today and arranges ambulance transfer to ED, with a phone handover to ED (not a private car, not outpatient follow-up).
While she waits, sits her upright and repeats observations. Gives oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%, targeting 92 to 96%.
Outlines the hospital plan:

kids.x: IV loop diuretic (furosemide), with monitoring of weight, fluid balance, electrolytes and renal function.
Transthoracic echocardiogram to measure the ejection fraction and assess the valves (including aortic stenosis).
Troponin and assessment for ischaemia as the cause or trigger.

check.d: Also credit if stated in the ISBAR Recommendation.

check.x: Mentions one longer-term step: heart failure program, cardiac rehabilitation or review of her post-NSTEMI medicines.
check.d: Any one earns the item. The full longer-term plan is in the teaching notes and is not marked.

check.x: Explains to Kathy in plain words, checking what she already understands, building on her biology background, giving information in small chunks without jargon and checking understanding:
check.d: Source marking: checks understanding, small chunks, avoids jargon and relates to her experience (she is a biologist). The communication style is marked globally within this item, not as a separate tick.

kids.x: Heart failure: the heart is not pumping well enough, so fluid backs up into the lungs. This explains the breathlessness, especially lying flat. It is probably linked to her heart attack and blood pressure.
Why hospital today: fluid on the lungs and low oxygen need IV treatment and close monitoring.

check.x: Safety netting
Gives red flags in plain words: breathlessness at rest or getting worse, being unable to lie down at all, chest pain, coughing up frothy or pink phlegm, fainting or confusion.
check.d: Credit if at least 3 specific red flags are named; a full list is not expected.

check.x: Says what to do if any of these happen: tell staff immediately while waiting here; after discharge, call 000 for these.
check.d: Both parts are needed: staff now, 000 after discharge.

part2.lead: After your examination the practice nurse recorded an ECG, and the GP arranged an urgent chest X-ray and blood tests at the on-site imaging and collection service. It is now 11:00 and she is back in the treatment room. Here are her observations, her ECG, her chest X-ray report and her blood results.
part2.patient:
Kathy is present for question 4. When the candidate explains, she asks, if not already covered:

  • "I'm a biologist, so I understand the basic anatomy and physiology of the heart. What exactly is going wrong with mine?"

She appreciates being spoken to as an intelligent adult and accepts going to hospital once she understands why. If the candidate uses jargon ("ejection fraction", "decompensated") without explaining it, she asks what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse on room air. Weight 70 kg today (67 kg 3 months ago). The 10:15 set was taken just after she walked back from the on-site X-ray room.
handover.model:
Read: at rest HR 102 to 104 regular, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air, BP 154 to 156/86 to 88, temperature 36.7 °C, alert. After a short walk, HR rose to 106, RR to 26 and SpO2 fell to 93%, returning to her resting values (HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 94%) after rest, but no better than on arrival at 09:30. Weight is up 3 kg in 3 months.

For Kathy: persisting tachycardia and tachypnoea with borderline oxygenation at rest, worse on minimal exertion. She is afebrile, which makes sepsis unlikely. Her blood pressure is raised but there is no hypotension or shock, and she is alert and warm. The weight gain fits fluid retention. On the NSW adult observation chart her SpO2 of 93 to 94% sits in the yellow (clinical review) zone at every set, and her RR of 26 after walking is also in the yellow zone; her HR of 102 to 106, though tachycardic, is below the yellow zone, and no value reaches the red (rapid response) zone. Her observations are not improving.

What it changes: she is not safe to manage at home, as her findings at 09:30 already suggested. Arrange ambulance transfer to ED, keep her upright and repeat the observations while she waits. Give oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%.

rows.note: Just walked back from the on-site X-ray room; breathless
Seated at rest in treatment room

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 09:50 today. Kathy Jefferson, 78.

  • Rate: 102 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm (sinus tachycardia). P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal (+10°).
  • PR interval: 168 ms.
  • QRS: 96 ms. Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (S in V1 plus R in V5 = 40 mm). No pathological Q waves.
  • QTc: 446 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: mild downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6 (repolarisation abnormality with LVH). No ST elevation.
  • Comparison: discharge ECG from 6 months ago (from the hospital letter) shows sinus rhythm at 72 with the same LVH and lateral ST and T changes. No new ST or T change today apart from the faster rate.

Conclusion: sinus tachycardia; LVH with repolarisation abnormality, unchanged from 6 months ago. No acute ST elevation, no atrial fibrillation, no heart block.
handover.model:
Read: sinus tachycardia at 102, normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QTc. LVH by voltage with lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion (strain pattern), unchanged from the discharge ECG. No ST elevation, no new Q waves, no AF.

For Kathy: LVH fits her long-standing hypertension. The tachycardia fits decompensated heart failure. There is no arrhythmia (such as AF) to explain the deterioration, and no new ischaemic change. An unchanged ECG does not exclude ischaemia after a recent NSTEMI.

What it changes: the ECG supports a cardiac cause. She still needs a troponin in hospital, and the echo will assess LV function.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect, taken at 10:05 today.

Patient: Kathy Jefferson, 78-year-old woman.

Clinical details: 2 months of worsening breathlessness, now on walking 5 m, with orthopnoea and PND. NSTEMI 6 months ago. Raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles.

Comparison: none available.

Technique: not rotated (medial clavicle ends equidistant from the spinous processes). Adequate inspiration (6 anterior ribs above the diaphragm in the midclavicular line). Adequate penetration (vertebrae just visible through the heart).

Findings:

  • Airway and mediastinum: trachea central. Mediastinum not widened. Hila enlarged and indistinct, in keeping with vascular congestion.
  • Bones and soft tissues: osteopenic. No fracture. No subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Heart: enlarged, with a cardiothoracic ratio of about 0.62. No double right heart border; the carina is not splayed.
  • Lungs: upper lobe venous diversion. Bilateral perihilar airspace opacification in a 'batwing' distribution, with diffuse hazy opacity through both lung fields. Septal (Kerley B) lines at both bases. No focal lobar consolidation, mass or cavity.
  • Diaphragm and pleura: both costophrenic angles blunted with a meniscus, consistent with small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions. No pneumothorax. No free gas under the diaphragm.
  • Extras: no lines, sternotomy wires, pacemaker or foreign bodies.

Conclusion: cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema (upper lobe diversion, perihilar alveolar and interstitial oedema) and bilateral pleural effusions, consistent with congestive cardiac failure. Infective change cannot be excluded within the oedema but is not favoured.
handover.model:
Read (ABCDEF; technique is given in the report): today's PA erect film, adequate technique. Trachea central, hila congested. Bones osteopenic. Cardiomegaly (CTR about 0.62). Upper lobe diversion, batwing perihilar alveolar oedema, diffuse lung field opacity and Kerley B lines. Bilateral blunted costophrenic angles (effusions). No pneumothorax, no free gas, no lines or wires.

For Kathy: this is the classic picture of congestive heart failure with pulmonary oedema and bilateral effusions. It matches the orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles and stony dull bases. There is no hyperinflation to suggest COPD, and no lobar consolidation.

What it changes: alveolar oedema with low saturations means hospital treatment today with an IV diuretic, and an echo to find the cause.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 09:55 at the on-site collection service; urgent results phoned through at 10:50. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: BNP 1,280 ng/L, markedly raised. Creatinine 104 (baseline 88) with eGFR 44, urea 9.6 and sodium 134. Potassium 4.4 is normal. Hb 128 with a normal MCV, normal white cell count and platelets. LFTs, albumin and TSH are normal.

For Kathy: the BNP strongly supports heart failure; a normal BNP would have made it unlikely. The rise in creatinine and urea from baseline and the mild hyponatraemia fit reduced renal perfusion in heart failure. A normal Hb and TSH make anaemia and thyrotoxicosis unlikely contributors to her breathlessness, and a normal white cell count argues against pneumonia. Normal LFTs show no significant hepatic congestion.

What it changes: these are baselines for the hospital team, who will monitor electrolytes and renal function closely during IV diuresis and when they start heart failure medicines.

rows.n: Acute presentation: BNP below 100 ng/L makes heart failure unlikely (non-acute threshold below 35 ng/L)

ask: You are now calling the emergency department registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Kathy, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, what is Kathy's NYHA class, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Kathy now in general practice, what you expect to happen in hospital, and one longer-term step.
Kathy asks what is wrong with her heart and why she needs hospital today. Explain this to her, and tell her the warning signs to watch for while she waits and once she is home, and what to do.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student at the practice with the supervising GP. Kathy Jefferson, 78.
  • Situation: probable new decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema. Sending her by ambulance; requesting ED assessment and admission.
  • Background: 2 months of breathlessness, now after 5 m, with orthopnoea and PND. NSTEMI 6 months ago, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia. Takes aspirin, amlodipine and atorvastatin. No allergies. Ex-smoker (10 pack-years).
  • Assessment: HR about 104, RR 22 (26 after walking), SpO2 93 to 94% on room air, afebrile. JVP +5 cm, S3, bibasal crackles and dullness. X-ray: cardiomegaly (CTR 0.62), upper lobe diversion, perihilar batwing alveolar oedema with Kerley B lines, bilateral effusions. ECG: sinus tachycardia 102, LVH with strain unchanged from 6 months ago, no AF or acute ST change. Bloods: BNP 1,280; creatinine 104 (baseline 88), eGFR 44; Hb and TSH normal.
  • Recommendation: IV diuretic, troponin, echocardiogram, admission.

Most likely: new, decompensated congestive heart failure with pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions, probably ischaemic and hypertensive. NYHA class IV (breathless at rest and on walking 5 m). For it: orthopnoea, PND, prior NSTEMI, raised JVP, S3, displaced apex, crackles, weight gain, X-ray findings, BNP 1,280.

At least two differentials, each with one feature for or against:

  • Aortic stenosis or other valve disease: age and risk factors. Against: no exertional syncope or chest pain, no murmur, normal carotid upstroke. Echo will confirm.
  • COPD: 10 pack-years. Against: no chronic cough or wheeze; orthopnoea and PND; oedema, not hyperinflation, on X-ray.
  • Recurrent ischaemia or ACS: recent NSTEMI. Against: no chest pain, ECG unchanged. Troponin needed.
  • Pulmonary embolism: against: gradual course, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf signs, and the X-ray explains the picture.

1. Disposition: NYHA IV, alveolar oedema and SpO2 93 to 94%, so hospital today. Discuss with the supervising GP. Ambulance (000) to ED with a phone handover to ED, not a private car.
  2. While waiting: sit her upright and repeat observations. Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92% (target 92 to 96%).
  3. Expected in hospital: IV furosemide; monitoring of weight, fluid balance, electrolytes and renal function; troponin; transthoracic echo for ejection fraction and valves; look for and treat the trigger.
  4. Longer term: one step, such as a heart failure program, cardiac rehabilitation or a review of her post-NSTEMI medicines.

Also credit a candidate who says that in real practice she should have gone to ED by ambulance straight after the examination, without waiting for the X-ray and bloods.

• Explanation: checks what she knows and builds on her biology background, in small chunks without jargon. Her heart is not pumping well enough, so fluid backs up into her lungs, which is why she is breathless lying flat. It is probably linked to her heart attack and blood pressure. She needs hospital today for IV treatment and monitoring.
  • Red flags: worse breathlessness, unable to lie down at all, chest pain, frothy or pink phlegm, fainting or confusion.
  • What to do: tell staff immediately while waiting here; after discharge, call 000 for these.

ddx.dx: Congestive heart failure (new, decompensated) with pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions
ddx.for: Progressive breathlessness now at 5 m with orthopnoea and PND, NSTEMI 6 months ago and hypertension, raised JVP, S3, displaced apex, bibasal crackles and effusions, 3 kg weight gain, cardiomegaly with batwing oedema on X-ray and BNP 1,280.

ddx.dx: Aortic stenosis or other valvular heart disease
ddx.for: Age 78 with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and progressive exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No exertional syncope or chest pain, no murmur and a normal carotid upstroke; the echo will confirm.

ddx.for: Former smoker of about 10 pack-years with exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No chronic cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND, and pulmonary oedema rather than hyperinflation on the X-ray.

ddx.dx: Recurrent myocardial ischaemia or acute coronary syndrome
ddx.for: NSTEMI 6 months ago, a family history of coronary disease (premature angina in her sister at 58) and new heart failure with tachycardia.
ddx.against: No chest pain, sweating or nausea and no new change on the ECG; troponin is still needed.

ddx.for: Breathlessness, tachycardia and SpO2 93 to 94% in an older woman.
ddx.against: Gradual 2-month course with orthopnoea and PND, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf signs, and an X-ray that explains the picture.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 09:30. Give orthopnoea and PND only when the candidate asks about them specifically. "Is it worse at night?" alone does not release them. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Item 9 follows the source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least five diagnoses from different systems, part credit for three or four. The heart failure questions in items 6 and 7 together count as one system.

Part 2 is set at 11:00 the same day. Hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Kathy is present for question 4 and asks her questions if the candidate has not covered them. Credit the chest X-ray read (item 24) in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer. If you show an image, use one without visible identifiers or a date, or crop the label out. The source expects NYHA class IV. A candidate who says class III should be asked to justify it, but item 28 is credited only for class IV. Also credit a candidate who says that in real practice she should have gone to ED by ambulance straight after the examination, without waiting for the X-ray and bloods.

The source offers two alternative question sets. This station uses the first: NYHA class, the top differentials, investigations and X-ray interpretation. From the second set, it keeps the communication skills in question 4. HFrEF has not yet been confirmed, because the echo is still to come, so the normal ejection fraction value and the full HFrEF and HFpEF comparison are in the teaching notes and are not marked.

A high-performing candidate quantifies the breathlessness by distance, asks directly about orthopnoea and PND, screens at least five differentials in clusters and picks up the NSTEMI. They examine the JVP, praecordium and lung bases. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically and name heart failure, NYHA IV. They send her to ED by ambulance and explain heart failure at the right level for a biologist.

A borderline candidate rates the breathlessness out of 10, misses orthopnoea and PND, or describes the X-ray without naming pulmonary oedema. They may start oral furosemide and plan a review next week instead of sending her to hospital.
explain:
Diagnosis: new, decompensated congestive heart failure

Kathy is 78 and has hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, a family history of coronary disease (premature angina in her sister at 58) and an NSTEMI 6 months ago. Her breathlessness has progressed over 2 months, with a sharp decline in the past week. She now has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, the most specific symptoms of left heart failure, and she does not volunteer them. Examination shows a raised JVP with a positive hepatojugular reflux, a displaced apex, an S3, bibasal crackles and bilateral effusions, and she has gained 3 kg. The chest X-ray, raised BNP and ECG confirm the picture. The most likely cause is ischaemic heart disease, with hypertension contributing (LVH on the ECG). An echocardiogram will show whether the ejection fraction is reduced or preserved.

Quantifying breathlessness and the NYHA class

Ask what she can do rather than for a score out of 10: running, walking around the block, walking to the letterbox, getting dressed or showering. This shows the effect on her life and gives the New York Heart Association class:

  • I: no limitation of ordinary activity.
  • II: slight limitation; comfortable at rest, breathless with ordinary activity.
  • III: marked limitation; breathless with less than ordinary activity.
  • IV: symptoms with any physical activity, or at rest.

Kathy has gone from 50 m to 5 m, and she is breathless at rest. The source classes her as NYHA IV.

Screening other systems

Group the associated symptoms in clusters for each differential:

  • Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, dry cough, RUQ discomfort.
  • ACS or angina: chest pain, sweating, nausea, syncope, palpitations, sense of doom.
  • Aortic stenosis: exertional syncope and chest pain.
  • Arrhythmia: palpitations, syncope.
  • Pneumonia or TB: fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic pain.
  • COPD and asthma: chronic or night-time cough, wheeze, atopy.
  • Interstitial lung disease: dry cough, occupational, chemical or radiotherapy exposure.
  • PE: haemoptysis, pleuritic pain.
  • Thyrotoxicosis and anaemia: tremor, weight loss, diarrhoea; fatigue and pallor.

Reading the chest X-ray (RIPE, then ABCDEF)

  • Rotation: medial clavicle ends equidistant from the spinous processes.
  • Inspiration: 5 to 6 anterior ribs in the midclavicular line, or 8 to 10 posterior ribs.
  • Penetration: vertebrae visible through the heart.
  • Exposure.
  • Airway and mediastinum: tracheal deviation.
  • Bones and soft tissues: fractures, subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Cardiac: cardiomegaly, chamber enlargement, aortic aneurysm.
  • Diaphragm: free gas, blunted costophrenic angles, flattening.
  • Extras: lines, wires, pacemakers, foreign bodies.
  • Fields: markings, opacities, oedema, nodules, air bronchograms.

Signs of congestive heart failure:

  • cardiomegaly, with a cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 on a PA film;
  • single-chamber enlargement: a double right heart border or splayed carina with an enlarged left atrium;
  • upper lobe venous diversion;
  • interstitial oedema, with Kerley B lines;
  • perihilar 'batwing' alveolar oedema;
  • pleural effusions, with blunted costophrenic angles.

Kathy's film shows cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, batwing oedema, Kerley B lines and bilateral effusions.

The other results

  • ECG: looks for the cause (ischaemia, LVH, signs of pulmonary hypertension) and for triggers (arrhythmia such as AF, new ischaemia). Kathy has sinus tachycardia and an unchanged LVH strain pattern, but a troponin is still needed.
  • Bloods:
    • A natriuretic peptide (BNP or NT-proBNP) is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain. A normal level makes heart failure unlikely, and a high level supports it. In an acute presentation, BNP below 100 ng/L makes heart failure unlikely. In a non-acute presentation the NHFA/CSANZ thresholds are lower (BNP below 35 ng/L, NT-proBNP below 125 ng/L). MBS eligibility for natriuretic peptide testing has historically been limited to the ED setting; check current MBS rules, as an out-of-hospital test may not be rebated. Australian laboratories most often report NT-proBNP.
    • FBC excludes anaemia.
    • UEC gives the baseline for diuretics and heart failure medicines; the creatinine rise reflects reduced renal perfusion.
    • LFTs look for hepatic congestion.
    • TFTs exclude thyroid disease.
  • Echocardiogram: the key investigation, measuring LV function and valve disease.

Differentials

  • Aortic stenosis and other valve disease: a common cause of breathlessness in older adults. There is no murmur here, but only an echo can exclude it.
  • COPD: unlikely with 10 pack-years, no cough or wheeze, and oedema rather than hyperinflation on the X-ray.
  • Recurrent ischaemia: must be excluded as a trigger after a recent NSTEMI.
  • Pneumonia: less likely with no fever, a normal white cell count and no lobar consolidation.
  • PE: does not fit the gradual course with orthopnoea and PND.

Management (NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline; eTG Cardiovascular)

In real practice, a patient breathless at rest with these signs can go straight to ED; the X-ray and bloods here are given for teaching, and investigations should not delay transfer.

  • Hospital care: acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema, low saturations and rapidly worsening symptoms needs hospital care. Transfer her by ambulance with a phone handover.
  • Oxygen: titrate only to a target of 92 to 96% (TSANZ). Routine oxygen is not needed if her saturation is above this.
  • In hospital:
    • an IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for congestion;
    • daily weights, fluid balance and close monitoring of electrolytes and renal function;
    • troponin;
    • a transthoracic echo;
    • a search for the trigger, including ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure and medicines.
  • If HFrEF is confirmed: guideline-directed therapy is started and titrated once she is stable. This means an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; a heart failure beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or nebivolol); a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; and, in current practice, an SGLT2 inhibitor, with loop diuretics for congestion. Amlodipine is neutral in HFrEF. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and NSAIDs should be avoided.
  • Post-ACS secondary prevention: note she is not on a P2Y12 inhibitor, beta-blocker or ACE inhibitor after her NSTEMI; check the discharge letter and review post-ACS secondary prevention.
  • After discharge:
    • a multidisciplinary heart failure disease management program;
    • cardiac rehabilitation;
    • daily self-weighing;
    • influenza and pneumococcal vaccination;
    • early GP review.

HFrEF and HFpEF, explained to a biologist

Teaching only: the normal ejection fraction value and the reduced versus preserved comparison below are not marked in this station.

Ejection fraction is the percentage of the blood in the left ventricle that is pumped out in one beat, normally above about 55%. The Australian guideline defines HFrEF as an LVEF below 50%, and HFpEF as an LVEF of 50% or more with evidence of heart failure.

  • HFrEF: a dilated, 'floppy' ventricle, like a floppy balloon, that cannot contract well enough to empty.
  • HFpEF: a normal-sized ventricle with thick, stiff (hypertrophied) walls that cannot relax and fill between beats. The percentage pumped out is preserved, but the volume pumped is still reduced.

HFrEF has a much wider range of proven medicines than HFpEF. HFpEF treatment centres on diuretics for congestion, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and managing blood pressure, AF and other conditions. Both types carry a substantial risk of readmission and death.

When you explain this, check what the patient already knows, use small chunks, avoid jargon, relate it to her experience (the fluid in her lungs explains why she can't lie flat) and check understanding.

Safety netting

While she waits, and after she goes home, she should seek help urgently (call 000 at home) for:

  • breathlessness at rest or getting worse;
  • being unable to lie down;
  • chest pain;
  • frothy or pink sputum;
  • fainting or confusion.

After discharge she should weigh herself daily and contact her GP the same day if her weight rises by 2 kg or more over 2 days, or if she has new ankle swelling. Arrange GP review within 1 to 2 weeks of discharge, referral to a heart failure program and cardiac rehabilitation, and involve her daughter.
points: Quantify breathlessness by what the patient can do (distance, stairs, dressing), not a score out of 10. This gives the NYHA class and the impact on daily life.

Always ask directly about orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, as patients rarely volunteer them. Screen at least five differentials across cardiac, respiratory and other systems with cluster questions.

Signs of congestive heart failure on a chest X-ray are cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, interstitial oedema (Kerley B lines), perihilar batwing alveolar oedema and pleural effusions. Read the film with RIPE, then ABCDEF.
A normal BNP makes heart failure unlikely and a high BNP supports it. The echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis and separates reduced from preserved ejection fraction.
New heart failure with pulmonary oedema, low saturations and NYHA IV symptoms needs hospital care today for an IV diuretic, troponin and echo, not oral diuretics and a review next week.
HFrEF is a weak, dilated ventricle and HFpEF a thick, stiff one. After discharge, daily weights, a heart failure program, cardiac rehabilitation and early GP review reduce readmission.
